factors.name: Branching and arc connectivity
factors.summary: Very high loadings of Average connector degree (0.98), Token split (0.96), Coefficient of network connectivity (0.95), Control flow complexity (0.91) and Maximum connector degree (0.88) show that this factor captures how many arcs attach to nodes, especially at splits and joins. Number of empty sequence flows (0.74) and Connector Mismatch (0.59) also load here but have notable secondary loadings on Factor 2 (0.52 and 0.36), and Connector Mismatch has a modest communality (0.47). With 51% of the variance, this is the dominant factor.

factors.name: Size and sequential, separable structure
factors.summary: Separability (0.83) and Sequentiality (0.82) load highly, together with Size (0.66). In this dataset, larger nets therefore tend to have more arcs between non-connector nodes and more articulation-free nodes. Size also loads moderately on Factor 1 (0.47), and Connector Heterogeneity is only weakly represented (0.41, communality 0.20), so the factor rests mainly on two measures. It explains 26% of the variance.

interpretation.overall: The data are well suited for factor analysis: Bartlett's test is significant (p ≈ 0), the overall KMO is 0.81, and every measure has an MSA above 0.6. Two varimax-rotated factors explain 77% of the variance. The first factor reflects branching and arc connectivity around connectors. The second combines net size with sequential and separable structure. Several measures load positively on both factors, which suggests a common tendency for all measures to grow together with net complexity.
caveats: The third eigenvalue (0.96) is close to 1, so a three-factor solution might also be defensible and could split the factors differently.
Density was removed by the MSA filter and Number of duplicate tasks was constant, so neither is represented in the factors.
Connector Heterogeneity has a low communality (0.20) and is only weakly explained by the solution.
Size (0.47/0.66) and Number of empty sequence flows (0.74/0.52) load substantially on both factors, even though they were not formally flagged as cross-loadings.
The results reflect shared variance in these 288 nets, which were mostly produced by discovery algorithms, and may not generalize to other model collections.
